title: Mughal Interregnum and Rise of Asaf Jahi Dynasty

concepts.partName: Fall of Golconda and the Beginning of Mughal Rule (1687–1724 CE)
concepts.bodyMd:
In 1687 CE, Aurangzeb conquered the Golconda kingdom. The last Golconda Sultan, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, accepted defeat and was taken captive, imprisoned at Daulatabad fort. He died there in 1699 CE, and his body was buried adjacent to his guru Shah Raj Kakkal's burial site near Khurdabad.

With this, the Qutb Shahi kingdom, which had ruled the Telangana region from Golconda for nearly 175 years since 1518 CE, came to an end. Golconda became part of the Mughal Empire, and the Telugu people were brought under the Mughal emperor's direct rule. The vast wealth of the Golconda Sultans — gold, jewels, silver, diamonds, and other precious stones — was taken into Mughal possession. The territories once ruled by the Golconda Sultans came under the control of Mughal viceroys from 1687 CE to 1724 CE.

After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 CE, his weak successors failed to control the Deccan effectively. Combined with the selfish conduct of the Mughal viceroys, this encouraged revolts among the people — Sarvai Papanna's revolt against the oppressive rule of the Mughal viceroys being one such act.

### Sources

Information about the fall of Golconda and the establishment of the Hyderabad state comes from several sources: Kafi Khan's _Muntakhab-ul-Lubab_, and the travel accounts of Ferishta, Tavernier, Bernier, Thevenot, and Martin, which throw considerable light on the events of this period.

concepts.partName: Early Mughal Administration in Hyderabad (1687–1700 CE)
concepts.bodyMd:
### Rahulla Khan and Zulfiqar Khan

Before leaving for Delhi, Aurangzeb appointed Rahulla Khan as a temporary representative of the Mughal emperor in Golconda. Soon after Aurangzeb's departure, the outskirts of Hyderabad city were attacked by the Marathas, who ravaged several villages, leaving the ordinary people without protection. Unable to counter the Maratha attacks, Rahulla Khan took shelter in Golconda fort.

Aurangzeb then handed over the responsibility of ruling Hyderabad to Zulfiqar Khan, who before 1687 CE had been the subedar of Bijapur and had settled the situation there.

**Zulfiqar Khan's reforms:**

*   He was an efficient military general and an able ruler, who strengthened the army and protected Hyderabad from Maratha attacks.
*   To consolidate Hyderabad's position, he undertook repairs of the forts of Kaulas, Elgandal, Koilkonda, Warangal, and Panagal, and stationed military forces at these forts.
*   He continued the fauzdars appointed during the Qutb Shahi period — most of whom were Dakkani Muslims — who held authority to impose and collect taxes from lands within a 10-kilometre radius of the Haveli Parganas.
*   To control the Dakkani Muslims and revolts from local Pindaris, Zulfiqar Khan appointed cavalry in the parganas and established special police stations.

### Fauzdars, Circars, and Local Administration

After 1687 CE, under the rule of the Mughal viceroys, there were nine fauzdaris in Karnataka: (1) Kaulas, (2) Elgandal, (3) Narsapur, (4) Kohir, (5) Bhongir, (6) Warangal, (7) Khammammet, (8) Chicacole (Srikakulam), and (9) Narsapur (East Godavari). Similarly, four more fauzdars were appointed in Cuddapah, Kurnool, Adoni, and Nellore in Rayalaseema.

On the east coast, Chicacole, Rajahmundry, Machilipatnam, and Nizampatnam were formed into Circars. For easy and efficient administration, each Circar region was divided into several districts, with each district placed under the headship of a 'Deshmukh'. Alongside the Deshmukhs, landlords (zamindars) belonging to the Velama, Kamma, and Reddi castes also played an important role in administration before 1687 CE.

**Revenue machinery:**

*   Deshpande prepared the list of land taxes and other information related to cultivable land.
*   Fauzdars, Deshmukhs, and Havaldars were appointed to collect various taxes from the people, working with the help of local zamindars.

### Zamindars under Mughal Rule

During the Qutb Shahi period, there were one or two zamindars in each district. These zamindars had the right to collect taxes from the local people and were also conferred titles such as 'Manne-Sultan' and other honours from the Sultan, which strengthened their position.

**Revolt after 1687 CE:** Taking advantage of the disharmony and violence caused by the Maratha attacks in the Deccan, some zamindars declined to accept Mughal superiority and revolted against them.

*   Important zamindars from Telangana who questioned the authority of the Mughal Viceroy came from Kaulas, Palvancha, Jataprolu, and Noorkoel.
*   In coastal Andhra, zamindari estates existed at Vizianagaram, Peddapuram, Mogaltur, Nuzividu, Vinukonda, and Kondavidu.
*   In Bobbili, Velama zamindars emerged strong; the families of Malhraju of Vinukonda and Manikyarao of Kondavidu were bitter enemies. The Vasireddi family took advantage of this rivalry and occupied Chintapalli, later occupying more villages in Guntur Circar. The most famous of the Vasireddi Zamindars was **Venkatadri Naidu**, during whose time Amaravati emerged as an important centre.
*   In Nellore, the zamindars of Venkatagiri, Chundi, and Muthyalapadu were strong.

**Poligars of Rayalaseema:** In Rayalaseema, the Poligars (palegallu) revolted against the Mughal officer Rustumdiq Khan, who suppressed the revolts of the zamindars and Poligars with the help of a huge army.

The zamindars and Poligars finally signed a peace treaty, recognizing and accepting Mughal authority in the region. Further, it was agreed between the Mughal viceroy, zamindars, and poligars that they should maintain an army, construct forts, and collect fixed taxes from farmers in their parganas — the zamindars in turn helping the Mughal viceroy with administrative matters. Consequently, peaceful conditions prevailed in Hyderabad by 1701 CE.

### Fiscal Reforms (1689–1700 CE)

Around 1689–1700 CE, the Mughal emperor instructed the Mughal viceroys in the Deccan to introduce new and innovative mechanisms for enhancing profits, maintaining the army, and meeting miscellaneous expenditure.

*   Mohammad Shafi abolished the 'Ijara' system during his diwanship, and prepared a list ('zaam-i-kamir') of all the taxes to be collected from every district.
*   As a result, taxes that farmers from coastal districts had to pay to the government increased from 10 percent to 13 percent.
*   Commercial taxes, sales taxes, toll taxes, market taxes, and others were also increased simultaneously; Chaudharis were appointed to collect these taxes.
*   The profits from Hyderabad increased to approximately 2.20 crores.
*   In 1691 CE, when the Mughal officers and employees humiliated the people of Pulivendula (Cuddapah district), the merchants of the place migrated to other provinces; the local officer, Mohammad Jaffar, later recalled the migrants by promising them special concessions, facilities, and protection.

In 1700, Khan Sifar Khan, appointed by Aurangzeb as the subedar of Hyderabad, died. The Padshah (emperor) then selected Prince Kambaksh as the subedar of Hyderabad, with Rustumdil Khan appointed to assist the prince in administrative matters. Aurangzeb had decided to make Kambaksh the ruler of Hyderabad and Bijapur, but Rustumdil Khan — who had held important positions in Hyderabad between 1687 and 1700 CE — developed differences with Kambaksh.

**Maratha attacks and unrest:**

*   Aurangzeb fell ill during this time and lost control over Deccan affairs. In 1702 CE, nearly fifty thousand Marathas under the leadership of Tarabai attacked Hyderabad and plundered it for three days, torturing and terrorizing the people.
*   The selfish Rustum Khan made a secret agreement with the Maratha army, paying them seven lakh rupees from the treasury — creating commotion and tension among the local Hyderabadi Muslims.
*   Soon after recovering from illness, Aurangzeb took measures to set matters right in Hyderabad and the Deccan. He transferred Riza Khan, the Fauzdar of Hyderabad, to Ramgir in Bidar.
*   Riza Khan, however, violated the emperor's orders — with his own army of ten thousand soldiers, he robbed travellers and merchants moving between Hyderabad and Machilipatnam, creating terror among the people and questioning the authority of the Mughal emperor.
*   Around the same time, from 1701–1702, severe drought conditions prevailed in the Hyderabad Suba. According to contemporary European accounts, nearly 20,000 people died as a result.
*   By 1704 CE, the people of Hyderabad had lost faith in the Mughal emperor. The Marathas ransacked the outskirts of Hyderabad again in 1704 CE, looting the people, and Maratha armies marched on Machilipatnam.
*   Unable to control the situation, the Mughal Fauzdar of Machilipatnam fled. Under these precarious circumstances, the East India Company came to the rescue of the people and local traders — with its limited army and a well-executed plan, it was able to drive away the Marathas.
*   The people subsequently lost confidence in the Mughal emperor entirely.

### The Six New Subas of the Deccan

After Aurangzeb's occupation of the Golconda kingdom, the Telugu people became an integral part of the Mughal Empire. Between 1687 and 1724, the Deccan was under the authority of the Mughal viceroys.

Aurangzeb's plan was to keep Golconda and Bijapur separated as two different kingdoms:

*   The **first kingdom** consisted of parts of Telangana and coastal Andhra, along with the Hyderabad–Karnataka regions.
*   The **second kingdom** comprised the Rayalaseema region along with Bijapur–Karnataka.

This arrangement led to the establishment of **six new subas** in the Mughal Deccan: (1) Khandesh, (2) Berar, (3) Aurangabad, (4) Bidar, (5) Hyderabad, and (6) Bijapur. Later, the Hyderabad suba came to be known as **Balaghat** or **Painghat**.

*   In the Balaghat suba, there were the Siddhavatam, Gandikota, Gutti, and Kambham Circars, which after some time were merged to form the 'Cuddapah' kingdom, under the control of Pathan kings.
*   The second suba spread from Guntur to Kaleman on the Coromandel Coast and was called the 'Arcot' suba, with Vellore, Jinji, and Thiruchirapalli joined to it.

concepts.partName: War of Succession and the Restoration of an Independent Golconda (1707–1713 CE)
concepts.bodyMd:
Aurangzeb died in 1707 CE at the age of 99. After his death, a war of succession broke out among his sons — Kambaksh (Deccan Subedar), Azam Shah (Viceroy of Gujarat), and Shah Alam (Viceroy of Kabul) — all three fighting each other to occupy the throne.

*   In 1708 CE, **Shah Alam** defeated and killed Azam Shah in the Battle of Jajau near Agra, and later crowned himself Mughal emperor as **'Bahadur Shah'**.
*   During this time, **Kambaksh** declared himself Sultan of Golconda in Hyderabad. By 1708 CE, an independent Golconda kingdom was thus reestablished, bringing together previous territories of the Qutb Shahi kingdom once again under one rule.

**Kambaksh's reign:** Local people hoped their problems would be solved under Kambaksh's rule. However, Rustum Khan had become his enemy, encouraged by the new Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah I. Rustum, overambitious, planned a conspiracy against Kambaksh; Kambaksh tried to implement Bahadur Shah's Farmans in Golconda, but ultimately deceived Rustum, killed him, and confiscated all his properties.

Kambaksh also looted the khazanas (treasuries) in Machilipatnam, imposed 'Jizia' in Hyderabad, and raised taxes — the merchants and traders of Hyderabad were terrorized by his atrocities. All classes of people grew resentful of his acts; Mughal officers and zamindars who had until then supported him stopped paying taxes and violated his orders. These conditions worsened further as a band of raiders took advantage of the situation to rob travellers on the roads — among these bands, **Sarvai Papanna** of Khilashapur (Warangal) was prominent.

By January 1707, Hyderabad had become an epicentre for Mughal politics: both Kambaksh and Bahadur Shah I contested for the Mughal throne. In the combat that followed, Kambaksh was defeated and killed, and Bahadur Shah I was crowned Mughal emperor.

**Bahadur Shah I's Darbar (1707 CE):** Soon after his coronation, the new emperor organized a People's Darbar in 1707 CE and invited several zamindars, including Sarvai Papanna.

The emperor not only recognized Sarvai Papanna as a king but also honoured him with a 'Robe of Honour'; in return, Papanna offered the emperor vast wealth. This honour displeased the local high-class Muslims (Shah-i-Nayath), who immediately complained to the Mughal emperor about him.

Bahadur Shah I ordered Hyderabad's new Governor, Yousuf Khan, to punish Papanna — but according to contemporary historian Khafi Khan, the Hyderabad Governor passed this responsibility to his military commander, 'Dilawar Khan'.

After the end of Qutb Shahi rule, Sarvai Papanna strived to liberate the people of Telangana from the rule of the Mughal viceroys between 1695 and 1710 CE. He made Khilashapur — located in the north-east of Warangal, 50 kilometres from Hyderabad in the Golconda kingdom — his main centre of activity. His struggle was mainly directed against the dominant social groups and ruling classes.

**Background:**

*   Sarvai Papanna's native village was 'Tarikonda', located 25 kilometres north-west of Warangal.
*   Papanna belonged to the 'Kallu gita' or Gaundla caste. From the very beginning, his aim was not to take up his caste-based profession.
*   This is evident from Telugu folk literature, in which Papanna, addressing his mother, is recorded as saying: _"Tying toddy pots to the palm trees, getting them down and getting a share in that is not my taste. My hand should fall on the walls of the Golconda fort."_
*   In a similar vein, a Telugu verse written in the first half of the 20th century notes that Papanna considered "toddy tapper" a resemblance of hard work, someone possessing good leadership qualities and knowing well the proper utilization of resources — such a person alone being eligible to occupy the Golconda fort and rise as leader of the various castes.

Various heroic acts of Sarvai Papanna as a rebel against Mughal rule, in the aftermath of the fall of the Golconda kingdom, are recorded in historic literature, folklore, and oral traditions. Aurangzeb's contemporary Khafi Khan also provides valuable information about Sarvai Papanna in his work, _Muntakhab-ul-Lubab_.

**Rise to prominence:**

*   Papanna's activities began shortly after the Mughal army occupied the Golconda kingdom. He constructed a small fort at Tarikonda and opposed the fauzdars and zamindars who supported the Mughal emperor.
*   He also worked for some time, along with his followers, in the army of Venkata Rao, the zamindar of Kaulas. He later moved to Shapur, which became his base.
*   The soldiers of the Kaulas zamindar attacked and arrested Papanna, but the zamindar later released him along with his followers.
*   By 1701 CE, Zamindar Venkata Rao accepted Aurangzeb's authority and gave away his army — for this act, he was given the position of 'Mansabdar' in the Mughal emperor's army, becoming the first Telugu zamindar to join the Mughal army.
*   Under these circumstances, Aurangzeb appointed Qasim Khan, the fauzdar of Kolanupak, to suppress Sarvai Papanna. In the battle that ensued between the forces of Papanna and Qasim Khan at Kolanupak, Qasim Khan lost his life — making the rise of Papanna an important issue for the Mughal empire.

**Confrontations with Rustumdil Khan:**

*   In 1702 CE, the deputy governor of Hyderabad suba, Rustumdil Khan, confronted Papanna with a huge army. Papanna's key follower 'Sarvadu' escaped, and the fort constructed by Papanna was partially destroyed — the Mughals, however, failed to achieve complete victory.
*   After Rustumdil Khan's return to Hyderabad, Papanna reached Khilashapur along with his followers and built a new stone fort in place of the old one, helped in this effort by Sarvadu and Purdhil Khan. Shortly afterward, both of these men turned enemies and killed each other; after this, Sarvai Papanna was recognized as the sole opponent of Mughal authority in the Telangana region.
*   In 1706 CE, Rustumdil Khan made another futile attempt to suppress Sarvai Papanna.

**Later years and death:** After Aurangzeb's death in February 1707 CE, a war of succession broke out among his sons. Considering this an opportune time, Sarvai Papanna occupied the forts of Warangal in April 1708 CE and Bhuvanagiri in June 1708 CE. During this period, he also greatly encouraged agriculture in the Khilashapur region, increasing his profits and replenishing his treasury.

After 1709 CE, war broke out between the armies of Sarvai Papanna and Dilawar Khan. In this battle, Papanna lost not only his army but also his fort; under these circumstances, he left Khilashapur along with a few followers and reached Tarikonda. In **1710 CE**, Sarvai Papanna fought valiantly against the armies of Dilawar Khan and died on the battlefield.

concepts.partName: Mughal Officers in the Deccan (1713–1724 CE)
concepts.bodyMd:
After Aurangzeb's death, his eldest son **Bahadur Shah** was made Emperor of Delhi, ruling from 1707 to 1713 CE. After him, the Delhi throne was occupied by **Jahandar Shah**, who ruled for less than a year, followed by **Farrukh Siyar**, who ruled from 1713 to 1719 CE. It was mainly during Farrukh Siyar's rule that the Deccan Suba and Hyderabad were placed under two efficient Sardars: **Mubariz Khan** and **Mir Qamruddin Chin Qilich Khan**.

### Mubariz Khan as Governor of Hyderabad

Farrukh Siyar appointed Mubariz Khan (Kwaja Mahmad), who belonged to the Turani clan, as the governor of Hyderabad in June 1713. Before 1713, he had been doing minor jobs but, due to his hard work, rose to a high position under Aurangzeb's rule; Kambaksh had appointed him as his 'Bakshi' (paymaster, military inspector).

As governor of Hyderabad, Mubariz Khan used his experience and efficiency against invasions led by the region's enemies, saving the people of Hyderabad and restoring peace and order to the province. He received several privileges and concessions from Emperor Farrukh Siyar that no previous governor of Hyderabad had received:

*   He acquired absolute authority to rule the coastal districts, collect taxes, and so on, in addition to the governorship of Hyderabad.
*   He gained full power to control Machilipatnam, Nizampatnam, Chicacole, Eluru, Rajahmundry, Kondapalli, Khammammet, the diamond mines, and other territories.
*   Farrukh Siyar also wanted to curb the power of Mughal officers in coastal Andhra who were trying to become independent — the emperor issued an important Farman cancelling the powers of Abid Khan, who had until then served as Fauzdar and Amin of Chicacole, and transferred this responsibility to Mubariz Khan, who became the sole authority in Machilipatnam and Medak fort and other places.

These changes encouraged Abid Khan not only to violate the emperor's orders but also to instigate a revolt against Mubariz Khan. Even before Mubariz Khan reached Hyderabad with his military, Abid Khan took his family members and huge wealth and sought shelter at Gandikota. Considering this an appropriate opportunity, Mubariz Khan sent his son-in-law Tala-Ullah-Khan to occupy all the provinces hitherto under Abid Khan's control — however, Mubariz Khan's attempts to completely suppress Abid Khan were not successful.

### First Victory of Mubariz Khan over the Marathas (1724 CE)

Soon after Mubariz Khan took up his responsibility as Governor of Hyderabad, the Marathas, under the leadership of Krishnamalhar, attacked Hyderabad. In a fierce battle on the outskirts of the city, Mubariz Khan's armies defeated the Maratha forces — nearly 150 Maratha soldiers died and more than 100 were injured. The Maratha army chief Krishnamalhar escaped.

During the same period, Mubariz Khan's army also occupied Elgandal fort and defeated Venkata Naidu, and successfully occupied Chengapetta fort — which Mubariz Khan renamed **Farrukh Nagar**, in honour of the Mughal emperor. In a similar way, he defeated the brother of Venkata Nayaka and occupied Gopalpet in Panagal district. These victories further strengthened Mughal supremacy in the Deccan.

**Subjugation of the zamindars:** Mubariz Khan also tried to make the Telugu Reddi, Velama, and Kamma zamindars, along with the chiefs of coastal Andhra, accept Mughal supremacy, collecting taxes and arrears of tribute from them.

*   He called the zamindars of Nuzividu and Eluru — Meka Appa Rao and Koldindal Ranga Rao — to Vijayawada and made them repay all arrears of tribute and accept Mughal supremacy.
*   In 1715 CE, Diwan Mohammad Jaffar, along with other zamindars, competed with the Hyderabad Governor to protect his position and privileges; these efforts were also suppressed by Mubariz Khan.
*   Based on orders from Nizam-ul-Mulk (Deccan Subedar), he confiscated the ships of zamindars and prevented their mercantile activities.
*   In September 1714, when Tularam of Kondavidu tried to rule independently, Mubariz Khan defeated him and established his authority over him.

### Treaty between Mubariz Khan and Hussain Ali Khan (1715 CE)

Between 1714 and 1715, several changes took place in the internal politics of the Delhi darbar. After the death of Bahadur Shah, the brothers **Hasan Ali** and **Hussain Ali** — known as the Sayyed Brothers — emerged as kingmakers.

*   Jahandar Shah was pressured by the Sayyed Brothers to replace Dawood Panni, the subedar of the Deccan, with the Turani leader **Nizam-ul-Mulk (Mir Qamruddin)**. Nizam-ul-Mulk was accordingly appointed subedar of six provinces in the Deccan in 1713.
*   In May 1715, however, the Sayyed Brothers again forced the Mughal emperor to remove Nizam-ul-Mulk from the position of Subedar of the Deccan. In his place, **Hussain Ali Khan** — one of the Sayyed brothers who had played a key role in placing Farrukh Siyar on the Mughal throne — was appointed Subedar of the Deccan.

With this, the Deccan and Hyderabad became the main centres for political intrigue and conflict. For nearly one year, a war of supremacy ensued between Mubariz Khan and Hussain Ali Khan. At last, Mubariz Khan won over Hussain Ali with huge wealth and tried to place his son as ruler of Golconda fort.

**Later campaigns and death:**

*   In 1717–1718 CE, Mubariz Khan invaded coastal Andhra and established his authority there.
*   Between 1718 and 1720 CE, he fought with the Marathas; in 1718 CE, he was defeated by the Maratha armies and finally made peace with them by agreeing to pay 'Chauth'.
*   In 1724 CE, the Battle of Shakarkhed (80 kilometres from Aurangabad in Berar) was fought between the Mughal forces of Mubariz Khan and the armies of Nizam-ul-Mulk. In this battle, the Mughal forces were defeated and **Mubariz Khan lost his life**.

concepts.partName: Role of Nizam-ul-Mulk in the Deccan (1687–1724 CE)
concepts.bodyMd:
One of the most significant events in Indian history was the establishment of the independent Hyderabad State in 1724 CE. This state was founded by **Mir Qamruddin Chin Qilich Khan**, popularly known in history textbooks as **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah** or the first Nizam. His successors ruled the modern Telangana, Andhra, and Rayalaseema regions from 1724 CE to 1948 CE.

### Family Background

The ancestors of Nizam-ul-Mulk belonged to Balapur village in the Samarkhand province of Central Asia; the family claimed descent from the first Caliph, Abu Bakr.

*   **Khwaja Abid Bujaro**, the first-generation member of the family to migrate to India, arrived during the rule of Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. He was admitted into Shah Jahan's court and won the emperor's confidence through dedicated service.
*   When Aurangzeb succeeded to the throne after the war of succession following Shah Jahan's death, Khwaja Abid joined his service. In 1687 CE, he lost his life fighting against the Golconda rulers.
*   One of Khwaja Abid's five sons, **Shihabuddin**, returned from Samarkhand to join Aurangzeb's service in 1669 CE. He participated in the wars between the Rajputs and Mughals on behalf of the Mughal army and gained Aurangzeb's confidence — the emperor conferred on him the titles 'Ghazi-ud-din' and 'Firoz Jung'.
*   Shihabuddin's wife was Saphia Khanam, daughter of Sadullah Khan (a minister in Shah Jahan's court). **Qamruddin**, born in 1671, was their only son; he participated in several battles alongside his father.

### Rise under Aurangzeb and Bahadur Shah

*   In 1691 CE, Qamruddin commanded the Mughal army to occupy the fort of Adoni. Aurangzeb appreciated his courage and bravery and conferred on him the title 'Chin-Qilich-Khan'.
*   Through his intelligence and bravery, he also became the leader of the 'Turanis' in the Mughal Darbar.
*   Between 1700 and 1707 CE, Aurangzeb's Prime Minister Asad Khan and his son Zulfiqar Khan dominated the Mughal court; during this period, Qamruddin worked as Governor of Bijapur.
*   In the war of succession following Aurangzeb's death, Qamruddin acted as a mere spectator. Bahadur Shah I, who emerged victorious in the war of succession, appointed Zulfiqar Khan as Subedar of the Deccan in 1708 CE; Zulfiqar Khan continued in this position until he was killed by the Mughal emperor Farrukh Siyar in 1713 CE.
*   In December 1707 CE, Bahadur Shah I appointed Qamruddin as Royal Representative of Awadh and as Fauzdar of Gorakhpur. After some time, Qamruddin stayed away from all types of positions due to the increasing influence of Zulfiqar Khan in the Mughal court.

### Subedar of the Deccan and Conflict with the Sayyed Brothers

In May 1713 CE, Mughal emperor Farrukh Siyar appointed Mir Qamruddin Chin-Qilich-Khan as Subedar of the Deccan; similarly, the Mughal emperor appointed Kwaja Mahmad (Mubariz Khan) as Governor of Hyderabad. By the time Qamruddin and Mubariz Khan reached the Deccan, there was political unrest, economic disorder, rebellions by the zamindars, and a weak army. Both Subedars worked hard to set these precarious conditions right and succeeded in establishing the Mughal emperor's supremacy over the Deccan permanently.

As Subedar of the Deccan, Qamruddin also strove to save the people from Maratha attacks and restore peace. He took advantage of the internal wars between Maratha Sahu (Satara) and Tarabai (Kolhapur), and stopped paying them Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. He arranged military camps in all the important cities of the Deccan Suba. Diwan Riyasath Khan supported Qamruddin in these endeavours; his aim was to rule independently, without interference from the central government.

**Removal and rebellion (1715–1720 CE):**

*   Between 1715 and 1720 CE, Qamruddin faced several problems. In Delhi, the Mughal emperor, influenced by the Sayyed brothers, discontinued Qamruddin as Subedar of the Deccan and transferred him to Muradabad.
*   The emperor appointed Hussain Ali, one of the Sayyed brothers, as Deccan Subedar, who then entered into an agreement with Maratha Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath, granting the Marathas the right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. In return, Chhatrapati Sahu delivered 15,000 Maratha cavalry to the Sayyed brothers.
*   Consequently, the Marathas and Hussain Ali established a competing government against the Mughal emperor — leaving Mubariz Khan, the Governor of Hyderabad, in an embarrassed and humiliated position, with no way to raise his voice. In 1718 CE, the Marathas invaded Golconda; Mubariz Khan paid Chauth and accepted the defeat.
*   In Delhi, Farrukh Siyar grew weak because of the Sayyed brothers' uncontrolled authority and carefully planned to end their supremacy in the Mughal court. Hasan Ali learnt of the plan and immediately recalled his brother Hussain Ali, then Subedar of the Deccan, to Delhi. Hussain Ali appointed his son Alam Ali Khan as his representative at Aurangabad and reached Delhi. Within a short period, the Sayyed brothers dethroned Emperor Farrukh Siyar and installed a weak ruler, Rafi-ud-din-Raza, as king, continuing their influence in the Mughal court.
*   In 1719, **Mohammad Shah** was crowned Emperor of Delhi. Nizam-ul-Mulk, the Turani leader, had observed these politics carefully and refused to extend his help to the Sayyed brothers.
*   In 1719 CE, the Sayyed brothers influenced the emperor to appoint Nizam-ul-Mulk as Subedar of Malwa. Sensing the Sayyed brothers' thirst for power and their treacherous acts, Nizam-ul-Mulk decided to attack them while stationed at Malwa, working to bring together their enemies and adversaries. Learning of these moves, the Sayyed brothers forced Mohammad Shah to remove Nizam-ul-Mulk as Subedar of Malwa in **1720 CE**.
*   This act encouraged Nizam-ul-Mulk to rebel directly against the Sayyed brothers and their supporters — he had decided that his future, and the future of his supporters, lay in his own hands. It was with this ambition that he took up arms: in **May 1720 CE**, he conquered the forts of Asirgarh and Burhanpur and openly questioned Mughal authority.
*   The Sayyed brothers, with the help of their supporters, dared to challenge Nizam-ul-Mulk but failed. In **October 1720 CE**, Hussain Ali was murdered, and Sayyad Abdullah was defeated and killed in battle by Nizam-ul-Mulk's followers. In this way, the Sayyed brothers and the Marathas were both defeated at the hands of Nizam-ul-Mulk's army.

With this, Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah appointed Nizam-ul-Mulk chief of the six subas in the Deccan.

### The Battle of Shakar Kheda and the Founding of Independent Hyderabad (1724 CE)

In 1722 CE, the Mughal emperor appointed Nizam-ul-Mulk as the Wazir. In this position, Nizam-ul-Mulk decided to strengthen the administration in the Deccan suba, but he faced opposition from selfish and corrupt officers from Rajasthan and from local zamindars. Even Muhammad Shah did not give him his full support.

Disappointed, Nizam-ul-Mulk decided to move from Delhi to the Deccan. Muhammad Shah treated Nizam-ul-Mulk's departure without taking his permission as an act of defiance, and ordered the then-governor of Hyderabad, **Mubariz Khan**, to either kill or capture Nizam-ul-Mulk and hand him over.

Nizam-ul-Mulk had already planned for confrontation and was ready. On **October 1, 1724**, in the historic **Battle of Shakher Kheda**, he defeated and killed Mubariz Khan, the Mughal representative, along with his army.

**Consequences:**

*   With this victory, Nizam-ul-Mulk emerged as the sole ruler of the Deccan and Hyderabad; the Mughal emperor did not even have the courage to oppose him.
*   Consequently, the Mughal emperor recognized him as an independent ruler — Nizam-ul-Mulk had become the founder of the independent Hyderabad state.
*   The victory at the Battle of Shakher Kheda earned Nizam-ul-Mulk the subedarship of the Deccan, the land with vast wealth, and Hyderabad. He received an annual profit of nearly 160 million rupees from the six subas.

Nizam-ul-Mulk ruled Hyderabad between 1724 CE and 1748 CE, recognized by the Mughal emperors as an independent ruler. The Mughal supremacy over the Deccan, which had begun in 1687 CE with the conquest of Golconda, thus came to an end in 1724 CE.

In the Deccan, the foundations of the **Asaf Jahi rule** were laid — a rule that continued till 1948 CE, bringing about several changes in the political, social, economic, and cultural spheres of the Hyderabad State and the Telangana region.
